original_query: Why were Eisenhower's two wins relatively weak compared to Harding, Johnson, Nixon, and Reagan? In hindsight at least--perhaps it was different at the time--Eisenhower seems to enjoy a broad degree of respect. Both liberals and conservatives speak fondly of him--as far as high-profile political figures in recent times are concerned, both Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump have done so, for example. And, unlike Dewey, Eisenhower was a non-politician. Dewey was a moderate, but I imagine it's possible he might have been put in a position to make decisions as Governor that could be used against him. Eisenhower, as the commanding general on D-Day, would seem to have commanded a respect akin to Washington or Grant. In 1952, Stevenson himself said, 'Who did I think I was, running against George Washington?' [1] But for all that, Eisenhower got 55.18% of the national popular vote in 1952, and 57.37% in 1956. While impressive, it seems like he had a stubborn floor that was higher than that of several other presidents before and after him, such as Harding, Johnson, Nixon, and, Reagan. The first three of these got over 60% of the vote, and Reagan got 58.77% in 1984. This is despite that all of these seem more controversial and polarising than Eisenhower (and also lacking the supra-political stature of having been a commanding general presiding over something like D-Day). Two things I can think of that might have hurt Eisenhower are 1) Eisenhower's non-denunciation of McCarthy in public, and 2) his running-mate choice (as Nixon had to give a speech defending himself against fraud allegations in 1952). But, whether they would have applied in 1952 or not, they would not seem to have applied in 1956. [1] https://www.americanheritage.com/why-we-were-right-ike
original_answer: Question: Why were Eisenhower's two wins relatively weak compared to Harding, Johnson, Nixon, and Reagan? Answer: Eisenhower’s victories in 1952 and 1956 were strong, but not overwhelming by historical standards. He didn’t reach the 60+% popular vote thresholds that Warren Harding, Lyndon Johnson, Richard Nixon, or Ronald Reagan later achieved. However, this was not a reflection of weakness. Rather, Eisenhower won in a deeply divided and partisan era where the structural conditions simply did not allow for blowouts. Too a lesser extent he did make decisions which cost him votes, some knowingly some rookie mistakes. Still Eisenhower’s strong victories were more impressive precisely because they occurred within such a balanced political landscape. In both elections, Eisenhower ran up against the enduring wall of Southern Democratic loyalty. The South—staunchly Democratic from Reconstruction through the Civil Rights era—remained a formidable obstacle to Republican dominance. Although Eisenhower, thanks to his immense personal popularity, made inroads in a few Southern states (a rare feat for a Republican at the time), the region remained mostly closed to the GOP. This was in stark contrast to Harding, Nixon, Johnson, and Reagan, all of whom benefited from periods of major realignment or collapse in the opposition party. By 1952, Democrats had controlled the presidency for two decades. Despite war fatigue and Harry Truman’s declining approval ratings, the party was still institutionally strong. Adlai Stevenson, the Democratic nominee in both 1952 and 1956, was an articulate and principled candidate who appealed to the liberal intelligentsia and urban working-class voters. The Democratic base, forged during the New Deal era, remained cohesive and loyal—particularly in cities, unions, and immigrant communities. In the mid-20th century, split-ticket voting was relatively rare, and partisan loyalty ran deep. Many voters who admired Eisenhower still voted Democratic down-ballot or simply stuck to party tradition. Compare this with later elections: 1920 in the first election where women could vote Warren Harding benefitted from Post-War Exhaustion, Backlash Against Wilson, and the collapse of the Democratic Party. In 1964, Lyndon Johnson benefited from the national trauma of Kennedy’s assassination and ran against Barry Goldwater, who was perceived as too extreme. In 1972, Nixon trounced George McGovern, whose campaign alienated moderates and blue-collar Democrats. In 1984, Ronald Reagan defeated Walter Mondale during a booming economy, in part because Mondale lacked personal appeal and ran on a platform of tax increases. Eisenhower, by contrast, never faced an opponent as weak or polarizing as McGovern or Mondale. His victories were narrower not because of any personal shortcoming, but because the opposition was still formidable. To a lesser extent, Eisenhower’s outsider status may have worked against him politically. Though widely admired as the Supreme Allied Commander in World War II, Eisenhower had never held elective office. He entered politics reluctantly and made several rookie mistakes. While courted by both parties, he chose the GOP, believing he would have more room to modernize and reshape a party that had been out of power for 20 years. He positioned himself as “above the fray,” which enhanced his reputation but may have cost him some political momentum. Notably, Eisenhower remained largely silent during the height of McCarthyism, even as Senator Joseph McCarthy attacked his former wartime colleague, General George Marshall. Eisenhower’s refusal to challenge McCarthy openly drew criticism from moderates and damaged his moral authority. His selection of Richard Nixon as running mate in 1952—intended to appeal to the McCarthy wing—nearly backfired. Nixon was caught in a financial scandal and had to save his spot on the ticket with the now-famous “Checkers speech.” The controversy sowed early doubts about the judgment and integrity of the Republican ticket. In the end, Eisenhower’s relatively “modest” vote shares given his immense and overwhelming popularity must be viewed in the context of a nation still politically balanced, with strong institutional opposition. He did not benefit from party collapses, massive realignments, or weak opponents. His strength lay in transcending those divisions—and winning decisively anyway.

original_query: How frequently is foreign press barred or allowed in war zones? (Yes, this is motivated by the question about press access to Gaza, but don't read support, or criticism, for that question in this one. Merely curiosity about how much we can expect free press access in conflict zones). To give some context of my understanding coming into this question: During the Vietnam War, the US, consciously or not, experimented with press freedom in a war zone. This was largely seen to have been a mistake from the US PoV, whether or not one agreed with war itself . From burning napalm on a child, to a self-immolating monk, to a spot execution of a bound communist sympathizer, a number of instantly-recognizable photos contributed in driving down US domestic support for the war. I kinda recall people stating that that access had been a) unusual and b) mismanaged. With the unusual aspect relevant to my question here. By Gulf War 1, the US had learned its lesson and the press coverage about press coverage was fascinated by the solution found: embedded journalists . Who were vetted, and controlled by, the Pentagon. So, yes, there was access. But, no, it wasn't free access. And, if I recall correctly, no one was much surprised or outraged, just a bit cynical about the press freedom quotient to be expected. In the Ukraine war, the press does have access to the Ukraine side of things. But even people highly sympathetic to Ukraine can understand that Ukraine has a vested interest in presenting its plight on the world stage. Free press access is of benefit to Ukraine, which is not doubt a huge part of the reasons it is allowed. On the Russian side of things, no, I don't think there is free access to foreign journalists to the occupied regions. They do conduct tours , of sorts, mostly with picked Western "journalists" of dubious quality. India has found it expedient at times to bar foreign press in Kashmir for months at a time. RSF in 2020 : "The Kashmir Valley, from which foreign reporters had already been barred for several months" Yes, there are plenty of counterinsurgency conflicts - presumably what Gaza is supposed to be at this point - where press is allowed, under various levels of control, by the official government. But in many cases, the "coverage of the coverage" also points out the reason: the government wants to appear strong and in control and a press blackout would give the opposite impression. Keep that in mind when looking at historical access to Gaza - just because it was allowed at one time doesn't mean the same calculation about the cost/benefit applies nowadays, from the Israeli side. Yes, at times Israel has allowed foreign press into Gaza, under highly controlled conditions, for example to show tunnels under hospitals. This is akin to Gulf War 1 embedded reporters and isn't generally seen as free press access. Guerrillas, rebels and sometimes even terrorists often explicitly covet coverage, consider press access a tool in their struggle and therefore allow it. But, like Ukraine, one should be under no illusion about why this is allowed, regardless of where one's sympathy lies. So, on balance is foreign press access the norm, or the exception, in conflict zones, on the government side? Especially by democracies, rather than authoritarian regimes. p.s. At the risk of stating the obvious, the press itself will almost always insist on press freedom. This question isn't about what the press thinks, nor whether public opinion thinks that the press should be allowed or not. It is concerned with what is normative/customary with regards to foreign press access in war zones. p.p.s. Be cautious about survivor bias here. Merely citing all the conflict coverage you can recall doesn't tell us much about the cases where it wasn't allowed. p.p.p.s. It was already in the comments, but it seems to have been missed: while it is motivated by the Gaza situation this question is explicitly not about Gaza : we already know the foreign press is barred there.
original_answer: I rather doubt you'll find a comprehensive survey on this that objectively manages to quantify the level of access. But to quote the nutshell from 2000 one : States frequently expect high degree of compliance from their media in wartime, usually rationalised on grounds of operational security and the protection of militarily sensitive information demanded by the war effort. [...] The British correspondent Max Hastings during the Falklands conflict famously remarked, "When one's nation is at war, reporting becomes an extension of the war effort. Objectivity only comes back into fashion when the black-out comes down". And yes, that paper agrees with you that the level of access that (US) journalists had during the Vietnam war was exceptional (and thus unusual both relative to precedents and to what came after), although that certainly didn't apply to connex theatres like Laos . The military in the first world was learning that you should handle the press by denying access and then acquiesce when they were ready to do a deal. Thereafter the approach has been used in Grenada, Panama and during the Gulf War. [...] The media management at Kosovo outdid that [Vietnam] record: he calls it the most refined model for journalistic death. There were 2700 people from the media accompanying the NATO forces when they entered the province at the end of the bombing campaign. There were daily briefings, military meetings, press conferences and endless arranged interviews all of which did not add up to news, but the journalists were kept too busy to notice. Much later, the stories they had missed, began to sink in. You'd be hard pressed to find a more comprehensive survey that you've already provided in your Q. You will find much longer discussions about objectivity (or lack thereof) from war zone correspondents. And if you'd rather read an equally long narrative about the press-military relations through the ages (but again rather focused on the US) there is one other chapter in the same book dealing with that. But you'd be hard pressed to find objective metrics of access used, and that chapter too often delves more into the issue of objectivity in reporting. And in lieu of any (more) statistics it has this (perhaps interesting) vignette as its conclusion section Pilger reveals that out of 649 journalists accredited to the Saigon press corps from 1968, only about eight of them made regular forays into the field (2001, p. 263). Jacques Leslie remembers it differently. He says that ‘most journalists, unless they were too frightened or concerned for their safety, got out of Saigon – the good stories weren’t in Saigon’. He takes credit for being the first American correspondent to go into Viet Cong territory, ‘only because of the arrival of the ceasefire in late January, 1973. Before that, it was impossible – anyone trying before that was likely to enjoy the fate of my friend Alex Shimkin, a Newsweek stringer, who blundered into Viet Cong territory in 1972 and was immediately killed.’ He does not see his actions as particularly daring or heroic. It was about being sensible and about being a good journalist. He had simply nurtured good contacts and sources, in this case Viet Cong sources, who assured him that with the ceasefire in place he would be safe and that he would be treated well. As he points out, ‘it wasn’t laziness on the part of other journalists that kept them out – rather, it was a quite reasonable fear of being killed, and the dearth of sources like mine.’ Once he set the example and showed it could be done, others followed his footsteps, some of them quite literally ‘to the very village I’d visited, until the village chief told them they were taking up too much of his time, and to pass the word to stop going there.’ The majority of journalists never considered meeting the Viet Cong because they had nothing to learn. The VC were the enemy, they were evil; end of story. Leslie’s bureau chief, George McArthur, ‘rarely left Saigon for any reason, relied on his CIA sources for many if not most of his stories, and probably figured anyone who pulled off the feat would be treated to nothing more than a Potemkin Village-like performance for his efforts.’ As for more recent conflicts... take this account I have a unique view of the war in Afghanistan, having spent much more time among Afghans than Americans. I arrived in 2012 to report for Reuters, when the US presence was winding down. I left after serving as the Wall Street Journal’s bureau chief in Kabul in late 2017, and continued to follow the war from Washington, DC, where I cover foreign policy for the paper. The US military refused to offer meaningful access in those years, so I often embedded with Afghan forces instead, or traveled alone with Afghan reporters, under the cover of a burqa where necessary. [...] Throughout this period, the Pentagon granted virtually no media access to US operations, and the increasing reliance on special operations forces happened out of public view. In the absence of a reality check, the rules of engagement remained designed for the fictional training mission the administration wanted, rather than what was actually happening. To be sure, the Pentagon’s resistance to allowing journalists access to complex and risky operational environments is understandable. And the media shares some of the blame: every major US television network pulled out of Afghanistan after most US troops left, and only a few newspapers were willing to continue the investment as reporting became more difficult. One of the problems for journalists trying to embed with Afghan forces in far-flung places was getting there in the first place. The US military often flew troops and supplies to these locations and could plausibly have taken journalists too (as it did in Vietnam, for example). But this never happened. Instead, when we embedded with Afghan forces in Kunar, or Nangarhar, or Kunduz, we drove to them in our unarmored Toyota Corollas at great personal risk. We made these trips as often as we could convince our editors it was worthwhile, but the lack of cooperation from the military hindered access for us and other media outlets. Put simply, the US military could have supported the media’s access to information about military operations in Afghanistan—information that would have contributed to a more informed and realistic strategic discussion back in Washington. But these decisions have to come from the top. [...] So yeah, complaint on one hand that the US itself didn't entertain journalists much in Afghanistan (at least during those latter years), but on the other hand, not a denial of access, if one could arrange it through others.

In addition, a new scheme addressing officials at local and county level (i.e. mayors, deputy mayors, presidents and deputy presidents of county councils) is expected to enter into force in 2021 (GO57/2019, GO 1/2020). The new law aims to scrap all special schemes and subsequently to integrate them into the main PAYG scheme, with the exception of pensions for military and police personnel. This makes me wonder why the concept of a special pension still exists. By special pension I mean retirement benefits not linked to social security contributions, often granted to certain public officials or specific groups under unique legal provisions. Details I understand that some jobs cannot be done until in your 60s (e.g. chasing criminals in the street, fighting in the front line). So, the general pension scheme cannot work for everybody, but the general pension scheme could be used with some tweaks. Examples: salaries could be raised enough for the people to be interested in that job, just like for the other jobs one year of work could gain more years towards the retirement threshold. Example (actually implemented where I live): anyone working in a dangerous environment such as mines, working with explosive substances etc. could get as much as 150% - 200% years towards the retirement threshold. Why are special pensions still needed in a modern capitalist state?
original_answer: Many pension schemes have simply evolved piecemeal over a considerable amount of time. There would often be special legislation and budgeting provisions. And the reason they have arisen is not always the same. The problem with rationalisation is that the government won't want to level things up, and the pensioners won't want things levelled down, so there will either be an increase in costs or an enormous political argument. Also, many special schemes have special provisions or laws applicable to the occupation they apply to. Notably, firefighters have a retirement age appropriate to their likelihood of maintaining physical fitness and mental agility (in a reaction-time sense, as opposed to the ability to process complex decisions slowly). Diplomats are more likely to have full spousal and family cover and exceptional benefits for death and various kinds of impairment - given that they often have to drag their families around the world and operate under a degree of risk. By time you've continued to account for special circumstances of many different occupations, and paid for all the legal, financial, and administrative analysis, then you're very likely to end up with a scheme that is about as complex as the ones you started with (and therefore rationalised in name only), but with needless upset and costs in the meantime.

The motivation for asking this question is that the US has a very expensive overall system for delivering health care. And, of course, if it was ever to be reformed the resulting savings - to consumers and to the government - would mean direct losses for some of the actors that benefit from those inefficiencies. Which means that they are incentivized to lobby energetically to avoid reforms. There are a number of cost drivers in health care: medicine: pharmaceutical companies, pharmacies and middlemen care delivery: hospitals, staff malpractice insurance health insurance: insurance providers, notably HMOs - Health Maintenance Organizations ) , which were originally intended as a cost-saving mechanism . HMOs - not supplemental health insurers - are a uniquely American, some would say uniquely rapacious, factor in health care. Some of those HMOs have just become giant profit centers instead and have every incentive to be involved in as many medical transactions as possible. Unlike the other components of health care, which can be rationalized and reformed but still need to be delivered to patients, HMOs don't seem to have a real reason for existence, in terms of patient outcomes or health provisioning. Which means that transitioning to a single payer system is anathema to them. And Medicare, due to attending to older people, means a lot of medical treatment, and thus lots of $$$, issuing from the government. original_answer: What's an HMO? An HMO is a type of Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C) offered by a private insurance company. When you have an HMO, you generally must get your care and services from doctors, other health care providers, and hospitals in the plan's network, except: Emergency care Out-of-area urgent care Temporary out-of-area dialysis Some HMOs are Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) plans that may allow you to get some services out-of-network for a higher copayment or coinsurance. It’s important that you follow the plan’s rules, like getting prior approval for a certain service when the plan requires it. Medicare Advantage (also known as Part C) Medicare Advantage is a Medicare-approved plan from a private company that offers an alternative to Original Medicare for your health and drug coverage. These “bundled” plans include Part A, Part B, and usually Part D. In many cases, you can only use doctors who are in the plan’s network. Plans often have different out-of-pocket costs than Original Medicare or supplemental coverage like Medigap. You may also have an additional premium. Plans may offer some extra benefits that Original Medicare doesn’t. Medicare is an insurance plan. However, Part A (hospitalization, etc.) is funded through taxes on wages and salaries. Parts B (doctors, etc.) and D (Prescription drugs) are funded by payments normally collected by deductions from Social Security benefits. Parts A, B, and D have deductibles and copayments (normally 20%). To protect against unexpectedly large out-of-pocket expenses, various additional insurance options are made available by for-profit companies. These include Medigap coverage (for deductibles and co-payments), Preferred Provider Organizations (PPOs), and Health Maintenance Organizations (HMOs). Each of these insurers accepts payments from their users and bills Medicare directly for services provided. Those not purchasing such additional insurance must satisfy any deductibles and co-payments before submitting claims to Medicare. Sometimes, if a doctor chooses not to accept Medicare's reimbursement amount, the patient must pay the doctor's fee and file a claim for the Medicare-approved amount.

It also reported that the impeachment will only happen if the South Korean constitutional court also upholds it: BBC (27 December 2024) : South Korea has voted to impeach its acting president Han Duck-soo, two weeks after parliament voted to impeach its President Yoon Suk Yeol ... Korea's Constitutional Court is typically made up of a nine-member bench. At least six judges must uphold Yoon's impeachment in order for the decision to be upheld. There are currently only six judges on the bench, meaning a single rejection would save Yoon from being removed. The Guardian has also reported that the trial of the former president Yoon Suk Yeol , for his impeachment, is also set to begin on 27 December 2024: South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol’s legal team are set to attend court on Friday as the constitutional court begins hearings into his impeachment by parliament over his short-lived imposition of martial law ... The court has 180 days to decide whether to reinstate Yoon or remove him. In the latter scenario, a new presidential election would be held within 60 days. The Wikipedia page on the Constitutional Court of Korea states: For passage, the [impeachment] motion must receive the support of a two-thirds majority if it concerns the president and a simple majority for any other office. Once the impeachment motion passes the National Assembly, the Constitutional Court adjudicates the impeachment, and until the Constitutional Court renders a decision, the impeached official is suspended from office and unable to exercise power. Involving the judiciary in a political process seems contrary to the doctrine of separation of powers in a democracy. As far as I am aware, most mature democracies tend to limit the scope of judicial review of normal legislative activities. Impeachment process, deemed to be a political process , thus also falls in the exclusive domain of the Legislature (i.e. the elected representatives are deemed to be the competent authority to adjudicate on such matters; criminal proceedings against the impeached official, if necessary, tend to be filed separately, and are often independent of the impeachment process.) original_answer: The logic behind involving the judiciary in impeachment questions is that a directly elected president should removable only if he broke some law (or is recalled by popular referendum , i.e. a kind of reverse election ), not at the arbitrary whim of the legislature, which can come up with a their own standard for "misdemeanors". Even the latter has yet to happen in practice in the US, it could happen in theory that the legislature removes the president because he has blue eyes or something. Of course, allowing the general electorate to reverse their decisions before the mandate term is up is itself a question of constitutional choice. Whether it's better or worse to have something remove at the popular whim is (also) a matter of opinion. In the South Korean case, it seems the president can only be removed if he broke some law. The legislature acts as a filter for referring cases, but is not the ultimate decider if the president broke a law . According to Article 65 Clause 1, if the President, Prime Minister, or other state council members violate the Constitution or other laws of official duty, the National Assembly can impeach them. Clause 2 states the impeachment bill must be proposed by one third and approved by a majority of members of the National Assembly for passage. By the Constitutional Court Act, the Constitutional Court must make a final decision within 180 days after it receives any case for adjudication, including impeachment cases. There is no popular recall option in South Korean constitution. Arguably, the proper separation of powers (if you insist on it) is that Parliament legislates, and courts apply the legislation. True, a Parliament could come up with very narrowly crafted laws to work around that like "anybody called Yoon must be removed from office immediately". But that's less likely to happen because of how silly it looks to the public which also votes in the legislature, so "legislative coup" like that isn't very likely. As you mentioned India in a comment, the president there (which less power than in South Korea), is indirectly elected by the national Parliament and the legislatures of the states. So, in that case it makes some sense that the removal process, which is more like a recall, happens at the same level. The US is probably the most special case, where the 'assembly' that formally elects the president is somewhat hard to ascertain. The Electoral College represents the will of the general electorate (so that's one level of indirection already), but their votes are further filtered by the actual legislature. So, in theory, the legislature in the US could also do a coup on that level by arbitrarily rejecting votes from some states etc. (mechanisms for invalidating flawed elections exist in other countries, of course. In some , it's again ultimately in the hands of the judiciary, for better or worse. As for a claim in some comments under the Q that this isn't common, it may be true in North America. original_answer: I think you're somewhat misusing terms here. Risk-limiting audits are conducted for some US elections. Typically these involve checking if a sample of the ballots were counted properly (as opposed to a recount, where the whole lot would be counted again). While the phrase "postelection audit" can be used to mean a variety of election validation efforts, as a term of art it refers to checking paper ballots (or records) against the results produced by the vote tallying equipment to ensure accuracy. Some details : A total of 49 states conduct some type of post-election audit. Alabama does not require post-election audits but piloted different audit types in the 2022 election. The most common type is a “traditional” post-election tabulation audit. There are also risk-limiting audits (RLAs), procedural audits, and audits that states conduct after an election that do not fall into either of these categories. More details on each type of audit are found below, but in summary: 35 states and Washington, D.C., require a traditional post-election tabulation audit: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Ohio, Oregon, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana (upon implementation of a new voting system), Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Of these, Ohio, Oregon and Washington give counties the option of conducting a risk-limiting audit instead and Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Texas, have had pilot programs to conduct risk-limiting audits. Six states have a statutory requirement for a risk-limiting audit: Georgia, Colorado, Maine, (pilot in 2024 and statewide in 2025), Nevada, Rhode Island, and Virginia. Eight states have other post-election audits that do not fall into the categories above: Indiana (procedural and/or traditional post-election audits may be authorized under some circumstances, with a pilot for RLAs) Michigan (traditional is authorized but not required, procedural audit, and had a pilot program for an RLA in 2020) Mississippi (procedural audit) Nebraska (not required but may be requested by the secretary of state) New Hampshire (randomized audit of ballot counting devices) North Dakota (post-election logic and accuracy test) Oklahoma (traditional is authorized but not required) South Carolina (data comparison) Traditional post-election tabulation audits are the most common audit type and look at a fixed percentage of voting districts or voting machines and compare the paper record to the results produced by the voting system. Even in a landslide election, they will count the same number of ballots as they would in a nail-biter election. Traditional post-election tabulation audits are usually conducted manually by hand-counting a portion of the paper records and comparing them to the electronic results produced by an electronic voting machine. In recent years, researchers have developed statistically based audit techniques that decrease the number of ballots to be audited, while also providing statistical confidence that the election result is correct. This method checks a sample of ballots (or voter verifiable records) that is guaranteed to have a large, pre-specified chance of correcting the reported outcome if the reported outcome is wrong (that is, if a full hand count would reveal an outcome different from the reported outcome). As defined in Washington, "a 'risk-limiting audit' means an audit protocol that uses statistical principles and methods and is designed to limit the risk of certifying an incorrect election outcome." In races with a large margin, fewer ballots need to be counted. If the race is tighter, more ballots are audited. States may have a process for ensuring the correct process and procedures were followed during the course of the election. This is referred to as a “procedural audit” and may be conducted instead of or in addition to a post-election tabulation audit. Procedural audits vary in their scope and comprehensiveness, but almost always include a ballot accounting and reconciliation process. In 2023, Utah passed a law requiring biennial procedural audits in addition to their traditional audit. The procedural audit is conducted by the Legislative Auditor General and may include auditing voter registration processes, candidate filing, ballot preparation and more. As you can see, checking the eligibility of the voters after they cast their votes is seldom done as part of these audits, although perhaps Utah wants to change that. I managed to find what Utah enacted (wrt voters' audit): (2) The audit shall include: (a) a random selection of at least .02% of the active registered voters statewide (b) at least one active registered voter from each county. (3) For each voter selected for the audit, the auditor shall: (a) verify that the voter is eligible for registration; (b) verify that the voter's registration information is accurate and supported by the documentation on file; (c) verify that there is a signature on file for the voter; (d) check for duplicate voter registrations; and (e) search available resources to determine whether the voter is deceased. So, the mandatory sampled percentage in each audit is pretty low (0.02%). N.B. it's officially called a "voter registration audit". TBH, IDK how it's different from the "purges" you've mentioned other than by name, and perhaps periodicity. Actually, the Utah audit doesn't seem to mandate removing somebody from the rolls. Just that the audit need result in a report identifying areas of concern. But presumably removing ineligible entries could be a follow-up action. So I guess that's the difference between an audit and a purge. So, states which conduct regular purges, and in which citizens need to re-prove their citizenship, implicity do such (voter as opposed to vote) audits. By the way, most of your examples don't pertain to elections annulled because of unqualified voters, but rather due to other kinds of irregularities/fraud. As for the Canadian example, it's somewhat less clear than you make it. The first instance appeal was successful on the grounds that records of voter eligibility were lost or misplaced by the state. It wasn't actually proven in court those people were not actually eligible to vote. So the Supreme Court erred on the side of not disqualifying votes because of a possible clerical error on behalf of (temp) state employees. In the US, non-citizen residents who register to vote are sometimes prosecuted . I'm not aware of an election where the (proven) number of these was high enough to change a result. The DA statement even stuff like: Noncitizen voting is an extremely isolated and rare event. Investigations in multiple states and nationwide have found no evidence of large numbers of noncitizens registering to vote. Even less common is a noncitizen actually casting a ballot. Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger launched an audit in 2022 that found over the previous 25 years, fewer than 1,700 people believed to be noncitizens had attempted to register to vote.
